💡 Key Takeaways
  • It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon.
  • To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results.
  • Industry observers note that "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, stated in a statement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It's no secret that NASA is working towards a permanent presence on the moon. The space agency even prepares to build a moon base for its astronauts to call home. But humans living inside lunar habitats around the clock will need three square meals a day, so researchers have been working on how to grow food on the moon.

To that end, a team from the College of Agricultural Sciences at Oregon State University have been raising potatoes in simulated moon dust with promising results. The researchers published their findings Nov. 20 in the Microgravity science journal.

Industry observers note that "We found that potatoes can complete their entire life cycle in simulated lunar soil when supplemented with organic matter," Aymeric Goyer, associate professor at OSU's Department of Botany and Plant Pathology, stated in a statement. "That's an key step toward developing reliable food production systems that could support long-term human exploration of the moon.".

To grow the spuds, the scientists used five different materials that are similar to regolith, the dust and rocks that cover the moon's surface. The moon contains various regions with unique surface makeups, so the materials they used simulated regolith from both lunar mare and lunar highland regions.

The secret ingredient was vermicompost, a soil that's rich in nutrients. The team added different levels of vermicompost to the simulated regolith to grow the potatoes. They figured out that fake regolith mixed with 30 percent vermicompost worked about as well as growing potatoes with regular soil.

"We believe the compost helps balance some of the toxicity we see in lunar regolith by reducing plant exposure to harmful compounds," David Handy, a postdoctoral researcher in Goyer's lab, said in the same statement.

In a recent development, the idea is that astronauts in the future could bring a little nutrient-rich soil with them and mix it with regolith to grow potatoes. After all, it'd cost a ton to ship all that food from Earth.

NASA funding supported this research.

Breaking: NASA’s Voyager 1 is now so far away that light takes 24 hours to reach it

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1646 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth.
  • The historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m.
  • The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

NASA's Voyager 1 has achieved another extraordinary milestone, becoming the first spacecraft to reach a distance of one light-day from Earth. After more than 49 years of traveling through space, humanity's most distant spacecraft is now approximately 16.1 billion miles (25.9 billion kilometers) from home. At that distance, even a signal moving at the speed of light needs an entire day to make the journey.

The historic moment occurred on November 18 at 2:16 a.m. PST (5:16 a.m. EST). Scientists and engineers at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, which is managed by Caltech, received a signal from Voyager 1 early Thursday, exactly 24 hours after the spacecraft reached the milestone.

The achievement marks another remarkable chapter for a probe that has traveled farther than any other human-made object, survived decades beyond its original mission, and continues to explore a region of space that no spacecraft had previously entered.

Voyager 1 Is Now 24 Light-Hours From Earth.

Astronomers often describe enormous cosmic distances in terms of how long light takes to travel them. A light-day represents the distance light covers in 24 hours, or roughly 16.1 billion miles.

Light moves through a vacuum at approximately 186,000 miles (299,000 kilometers) per second. To put Voyager 1's distance in perspective, sunlight passing Earth takes only about 1.3 seconds to reach the Moon. Reaching Neptune takes roughly four hours, while traveling from Neptune to Voyager 1 requires another 20 hours.

It has been revealed that even these enormous distances are small compared with those separating stars. A single light-year, the distance light travels in one year, measures approximately 5.88 trillion miles (9.46 trillion kilometers).

Voyager 1's extraordinary distance also creates a major challenge for mission controllers. Sending a command to the spacecraft now requires 24 hours, and receiving a response takes another 24 hours. A complete exchange therefore spans two full days, even though the signals travel at the fastest speed possible.

The milestone comes as engineers investigate a communication problem. NASA has not received scientific or engineering data from Voyager 1 since November 14. However, the probe continues transmitting a carrier signal, the radio signal that normally carries information back to Earth. By tracking this signal and calculating the spacecraft's trajectory, mission specialists were able to verify that Voyager 1 had crossed the one light-day mark. Engineers are continuing to investigate why the expected data is not coming through.

A Historic Journey Beyond the Solar System's Planets.

Voyager 1 and its twin, Voyager 2, were launched in 1977 to take advantage of an unusual arrangement of the outer planets. The alignment allowed the spacecraft to use planetary gravity to travel from one destination to another, making an ambitious exploration mission possible.

Managed by JPL, the Voyagers became the third and fourth spacecraft to visit Jupiter and Saturn. They also delivered the first high-resolution images of these distant planets, revealing extraordinary latest details about their atmospheres, rings, and moons. Voyager 2 continued farther, becoming the first spacecraft to explore Uranus and Neptune up close.

Industry observers note that today, both probes are traveling through interstellar space, making them humanity's only spacecraft to have crossed into the region beyond the Sun's protective bubble. Their instruments continue monitoring changes in the Sun's magnetic field across immense distances, providing scientists with measurements that cannot be collected from Earth.

"Traveling a light-day is a singular feat for a spacecraft, but Voyager is so much more than a distant traveler. The Voyager mission would be remarkable just for what it contributed to planetary science with the Grand Tour of the outer planets," noted Joe Westlake, director, Heliophysics Division at NASA Headquarters in Washington. "But it went on to become central to NASA's fleet of heliophysics missions offering insights into the star that we all revolve around, the Sun.".

"Voyager 1 crossing the light-day threshold is yet another historic feat on an extraordinary voyage of discovery," said Dave Gallagher, JPL director. "Above all, this milestone stands as a testament to the exceptional teams who built, programmed, and fly these spacecraft today, and who have overcome countless challenges to keep them connected to Earth across the vastness of space. As NASA pushes toward newly introduced frontiers in human and robotic exploration, Voyager and the people behind its success continue to inspire us to reach farther and dream bigger.".

Voyager's Golden Record Carries a Message From Earth.

According to recent reports, the Voyager spacecraft carry more than scientific instruments. Each also holds a Golden Record, a gold-plated copper phonograph record containing images and sounds representing life on Earth. These recordings were designed as messages that an advanced extraterrestrial civilization might discover someday.

The records give the mission a purpose extending far beyond its scientific discoveries. Even after the spacecraft eventually lose the ability to communicate with Earth, they will continue traveling through space with a small collection of sights and sounds from the planet that introduced them.

"Nearly half a century after leaving Earth, the Voyager mission continues to push the boundaries of human exploration. Its epic journey reflects the vision of Ed Stone, the Caltech physicist and JPL director who guided the mission for decades, and the curiosity and tenacity of generations of scientists and engineers who have carried that vision forward," said Ray Jayawardhana, president, Caltech. "Beyond its immense contributions to science, Voyager also captures something profound about the human spirit. We may never know where its journey will ultimately lead, but it will venture on, an enduring affirmation that humanity was here and we yearned to explore.".

Exploring the Mysterious Region Beyond the Sun.

Industry observers note that voyager 1 is at the moment moving through space at approximately 38,000 mph (61,155 kph). In 2012, it became the first spacecraft to cross the boundary of the heliosphere, a vast region surrounding the Sun that is filled with particles and magnetic fields generated by our star.

This protective bubble helps shield the solar system from cosmic radiation arriving from elsewhere in the galaxy. Beyond its outer boundary lies interstellar space, where particles and magnetic fields from the broader galaxy become more dominant.

Recent findings suggest that voyager 2 followed a different route and crossed into interstellar space in 2018. Together, the probes are providing the first direct observations of conditions beyond the heliosphere.

Recent findings suggest that one of their most intriguing discoveries is that the Sun's effects do not simply disappear at the boundary. Its influence appears to extend much farther into interstellar space than scientists once understood, raising latest questions about where the environment shaped by our star truly gives way to the surrounding galaxy.

It has been revealed that "The Voyagers are revolutionizing our understanding of interstellar space, a previously unexplored region outside the heliosphere," said Linda Spilker, Voyager project scientist at JPL. "One major surprise is the extent to which our Sun continues to affect interstellar space, all the way out to Voyager 1. Where does the Sun's influence end and pristine interstellar space begin? Perhaps Voyager may endure long enough to answer that question.".

How NASA Is Keeping Voyager 1 Alive After Nearly 50 Years.

Industry observers note that operating spacecraft built nearly half a century ago requires increasingly inventive engineering. Both Voyagers have experienced problems as their equipment ages, including clogged thrusters and a malfunctioning computer. NASA engineers have repeatedly developed solutions that allow the probes to continue working despite these setbacks.

It has been revealed that electricity has become one of the mission's greatest limitations. Earlier in 2026, engineers took a calculated risk by switching off three devices aboard Voyager 1 and replacing them with three alternatives that consume less power. This change was intended to help the spacecraft stretch its remaining energy supply.

It has been revealed that voyager 1 depends on a radioisotope thermal generator that is now approximately 50 years old. Often described as a nuclear battery, the device produces electricity by converting heat released during the radioactive decay of plutonium.

Industry observers note that as the radioactive material continues to decay, the available power gradually decreases. Both Voyager spacecraft lose approximately four watts of electrical output every year, forcing engineers to make difficult decisions about which systems can remain operational.

The latest conservation measures are expected to provide enough power to operate the spacecraft's current scientific instruments until at least the summer of 2027, when both probes will celebrate their 50th launch anniversaries.

One Day, Voyager 1 Will Become a Silent Messenger to the Stars.

Maintaining contact across such staggering distances requires some of NASA's most powerful communications equipment. The agency relies on its Deep Space Network, a worldwide system of large radio antennas located at three facilities, to communicate with Voyager and other spacecraft traveling to and beyond the Moon.

Despite the enormous communication delay and the spacecraft's aging systems, engineers continue monitoring Voyager 1 daily and transmitting instructions every week. The mission remains an extraordinary demonstration of what long-term spacecraft engineering can achieve.

"We listen to Voyager 1 every day and send commands to the spacecraft weekly. It just takes a little longer to communicate than it used to," noted Suzanne Dodd, Voyager project manager at JPL. "Even traveling at the speed of light, signals now take 24 hours to reach the spacecraft and 24 hours to reach us. One day in the future, when it can no longer communicate with Earth, Voyager 1 will become humanity's silent ambassador to the stars.".

Tidal is outlawing wholly AI-generated music from its platform, the streaming service announced on Tuesday, saying that AI music “diverts streams and royalties away from the artists, and confuses fans.”.

According to recent reports, “To ensure Tidal remains the best place for artists to share their work, and for listeners to enjoy it, we’re removing all tracks that we determine are 100% AI generated,” Tidal noted in a social media post on Tuesday. “We’re also banning distributors from delivering these tracks to us, and will reject deliveries if their metadata states they were generated solely using AI tools.”.

Sources indicate that tracks that were made with assistance from AI will still be allowed. The latest ban will go into effect December 9.

In a recent development, tidal said it’s seen an influx of AI-generated tracks on its platform over the past several months, noting that in the past 90 days, about 43 percent of tracks distributed on the platform were identified as wholly AI-generated. On Nov. 6 alone, 60 percent of newly uploaded songs were AI tracks. But despite the growing number of songs, 96 percent of those tracks have generated zero streams.

With its decision Tuesday, Tidal now has the most stringent anti-AI policies among the music streaming services, and one of the few notable platforms beyond Bandcamp, the music distribution service popular among indie artists, to have outright banned AI music. While Spotify and Apple Music, the two largest DSPs, have taken steps to either label AI tracks and artists or remove them from recommendations, they still allow fully-generated songs to get uploaded to their respective platforms.

It has been revealed that fans and the music industry alike have voiced their frustration about AI music flooding streaming platforms. On an earnings call in October, Universal Music Group CEO Lucian Grainge advocated for streaming services to pay out AI-generated tracks less than music from human artists, arguing that AI slop degrades the fan experience and diverts value from real artists,” and that removing the profit motive would disincentivize “industrial scale content production.”.

In the last moments of Dig's premiere, archaeologists Elise (Amy Poehler) and Dylan (Geraldine Viswanathan) stumble upon an astounding discovery. At the bottom of a trench that no archaeologist has touched in a decade, under a thin layer of dirt, there lie the remains of a perfectly preserved statue.

According to recent reports, "We dug in this trench for two years," Elise marvels. "And if we had only gone an inch deeper...".

She trails off, but the sentiment is clear: If the dig team had kept chipping away at the trench, they would have found the artifact of a lifetime. This scene is Dig's core thesis in a nutshell: You can always dig deeper and find greater rewards, whether it's in your relationships, your career, or yes, the giant trenches peppering an archaeological dig.

"Digging a little deeper is just good life advice in general, but it's also a really good lesson in writing," Dig co-creator Mike Schur told Mashable over a Zoom interview.

According to recent reports, writing, as Schur can attest, is "exhausting" work. "By creative standards, not digging a ditch standards," he noted. That means that it can sometimes be tempting to take the easy way out. To leave the trench after two years of digging, as it were.

According to recent reports, "When you hit on something like a joke or a scene or a character that's pretty good, every ounce of your being is like, 'It's good. Just move on,'" Schur said.

However, Schur learned to curb that impulse while writing on the American version of The Office, which was developed by his mentor, Greg Daniels.

During script revisions, Schur recalled the writers' room going over scenes time and again with a fine-toothed comb, punching up jokes, pitching latest ideas, and just generally refining what was on the page.

After revisions, Schur remarked, "I remember [Daniels] would say, 'Okay, I think that's two percent better.".

Recent findings suggest that schur continued: "He used to say that if you make every joke in the episode two percent better, then the whole episode is going to be seven and a half percent better, and that's amazing. You just made something a little better and a little more memorable.".

According to recent reports, think of that two percent as being the last little inch of dirt separating Elise from the miraculously intact Greek statue. It might be tough to excavate any further, especially if you've already been digging fruitlessly for years. But for writers, established and aspiring alike, couldn't that extra little bit of effort be worth it if you eventually strike gold?

As Schur put it, "Digging a little, doing a little extra work, revisiting a scene one more time to make it a little better is the essence of what I think differentiates memorable writing from very good writing.".

#173508. A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1830 w)

A giant star swallowed another star. James Webb reveals the aftermath

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1830 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it.
  • Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger.
  • Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Astronomers have uncovered an extraordinary stellar collision in the neighboring Andromeda galaxy, where a smaller star spiraled into a gigantic supergiant and ultimately merged with it. The rare event, the first of its kind to be identified, left behind a single star that may have been given a new lease on life.

Researchers have nicknamed the resulting star Bao, describing it as potentially "rejuvenated" by the merger. The smaller star was slightly less massive than our Sun, while its enormous companion was a swollen supergiant. The dramatic encounter took place near the outer edge of Andromeda and was investigated through a NASA-funded research effort.

Observations from NASA's James Webb Space Telescope provided crucial evidence of what happened. By combining Webb's findings with years of measurements from ground-based and space telescopes, scientists were able to reconstruct the stars' remarkable transformation.

Sources indicate that "Stellar mergers are very, very difficult to observe in real time because they are hard to predict," remarked Viraj Karambelkar, the first author of a new paper in Nature and a NASA Hubble Fellow at Columbia University in New York. "However, we noticed something unusual was going on in 2023 and continued to monitor the system to see what it would do. Then, in 2025, it erupted! Webb observed Bao only 47 days after the stars' eruption peaked, the earliest ever follow-up of an event like this. The telescope's data helped us characterize what the system looked like before, during, and immediately after the merger, which is absolutely mind-blowing.".

How a Giant Star Swallowed Its Companion.

According to recent reports, for thousands of years, the two stars existed as a binary system, orbiting one another without merging. That long period of relative stability ended when the smaller star began brushing against the enormous outer atmosphere of its companion.

Once that interaction started, the process moved surprisingly swiftly. The two stars completed their "unification" after just seven additional orbits (about seven years). Previously observed mergers involving pairs of smaller stars had required thousands of orbits to reach the same outcome.

The speed of the final eruption also caught astronomers off guard.

Industry observers note that "We thought an outburst from such an extended star would take years," said co-author Nadia Blagorodnova, an associate professor at the University of Barcelona in Spain. "One day, its brightness started rising and within a week, it peaked!".

Sources indicate that scientists had already detected subtle warning signs before the eruption. As the smaller star moved through the giant's outer atmosphere, it disturbed the surrounding gas and began stripping away material, gradually changing the system's brightness.

"When a companion star begins to interact with the outer surface of the primary star, it produces a subtle effect -- a slow brightening, which we clearly saw in Bao's data," remarked co-author Kishalay De, an assistant professor at Columbia University in Fresh York. "As the companion continues its orbit, it keeps peeling off the primary star's outer layers, and that gas flows away into the surrounding space.".

A Violent Stellar Merger With More Than One Possible Outcome.

It has been revealed that this kind of interaction is part of a process astronomers call common envelope evolution. It occurs when two stars become surrounded by a shared outer layer of gas, typically after one star expands enough to engulf its companion.

Sources indicate that as the smaller star moves through that gas, resistance slows its orbit and drains away orbital energy. The companion can then spiral progressively deeper toward the center of the larger star.

For Bao, the smaller star ultimately plunged inward and merged with the giant. Webb's observations provided the evidence needed to confirm that the stars had become one.

In a recent development, but such encounters do not always end with a merger. Sometimes, both stars survive, losing substantial amounts of material while emerging as two separate objects locked in much tighter orbits.

Industry observers note that these surviving systems are crucial because they can eventually produce some of the universe's most extreme phenomena. Depending on how the stars evolve, they may become neutron stars or black holes, undergo violent supernovae, generate gravitational waves that ripple through space-time, or form rapidly rotating objects called millisecond pulsars.

Understanding common envelope evolution is therefore essential to explaining how many of these extraordinary cosmic objects come into existence.

Reconstructing the Collision With James Webb.

To understand exactly what happened to Bao, the researchers refined computer simulations of the two stars and compared the results with Webb's observations.

The telescope's mid-infrared measurements were particularly valuable because they revealed dust that the giant star had expelled over hundreds of years. Infrared light allows astronomers to study material that can be difficult to detect at visible wavelengths, offering clues about the system's history long before its final eruption.

Recent findings suggest that the simulations revealed that the larger star had been truly enormous. Before the merger, it was approximately seven times as massive as the Sun, had a radius 350 times larger, and shone with 18,000 times the Sun's brightness.

Those staggering proportions earned it the nickname "Big Bao.".

It has been revealed that "It was an absolute beast of a star, completely outshining its companion in the data," noted co-author Karel Temmink, a Ph.D. student at Radboud University in Nijmegen, Netherlands, who led the simulations.

The researchers also calculated the mass of the smaller star for the first time. Nicknamed "Little Bao," it was likely somewhat smaller and dimmer than the Sun, with an estimated mass of (about 0.7 solar masses). In other words, it contained roughly 70% as much mass as our star.

At first, the simulations suggested that the smaller companion might have retained enough energy to "flee" the giant's gravitational grip and escape the encounter.

In a recent development, further investigation, however, revealed a very different ending. Little Bao had been dragged deep into the core of Big Bao, releasing an immense amount of energy as the two stars merged.

Their final encounter was "almost like a bomb exploding inside a living star," De remarked.

The merger has left astronomers with another key question: What is Bao like now?

The surviving star contains the legacy of both original stars, but its final structure and mass distribution remain uncertain. Future observations will be needed to determine how its "heft" settles as the newly merged object evolves.

Years of Telescope Observations Reveal the Warning Signs.

One reason this discovery is so valuable is that scientists had been watching Bao long before its dramatic eruption.

Sources indicate that although Webb supplied crucial information about the amount of material expelled and how efficiently the common envelope process unfolded, the team also drew on ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared observations from multiple observatories. Together, these measurements provided a detailed record of the system's changing behavior as the merger approached and unfolded.

According to recent reports, the researchers had even published an earlier study shortly before the stars erupted. (In fact, they published their first paper right before the eruption in 2025.).

The first major clue appeared in February 2023, when astronomers examining archived observations from NASA's retired NEOWISE (Near-Earth Object Wide-Field Infrared Survey Explorer) mission noticed a star whose brightness was behaving unusually.

Earlier records showed that the object had maintained a steady luminosity before 2018. Its later variations suggested that something significant was beginning to change.

By September 2024, observations from the Wide-field Infrared Transient Explorer (WINTER) showed further evidence of activity. The system was growing brighter and releasing dust into the surrounding space.

Another crucial development came in July 2025, when NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer) happened to observe Bao during a routine sky survey.

According to recent reports, the telescope detected a striking change: Bao was rapidly fading in visible light while simultaneously becoming brighter in infrared light. This unusual combination provided another sign that the system was undergoing a major transformation.

Recent findings suggest that then, on October 17, 2025, the Zwicky Transient Facility detected the eruption. The observations revealed a sudden surge in brightness accompanied by a dramatic increase in temperature.

In a recent development, scientists quickly arranged additional observations to capture the unfolding event. In November 2025, NASA's now-retired Neil Gehrels Swift Observatory and NOIRLab's Gemini North telescope in Hawaii supplied valuable newly introduced measurements.

According to recent reports, webb joined the effort on December 24, 2025, through an urgently approved Director's Discretionary Time program. This special observing opportunity allowed the telescope to examine the aftermath while the system was still undergoing rapid changes.

A New Window Into the Lives and Deaths of Stars.

The successful investigation of Bao, officially designated AT 2025abao, represents an important advance in the study of stellar mergers.

Rather than trying to reconstruct a cosmic event that occurred hundreds, thousands, or even millions of years earlier, astronomers were able to observe and analyze the process as it happened.

That timing made it possible to measure how efficiently the common envelope interaction transferred energy and expelled material from the system. Such measurements can help researchers improve their models of how binary stars evolve and what determines whether they merge or survive.

The discovery also arrives at an especially promising time for astronomy.

NASA's recently released Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope is preparing to carry out extensive publicly available surveys that could reveal many more unusual stellar events.

In a recent development, one of its major observing programs, the Galactic Bulge Time-Domain Survey, will repeatedly monitor large numbers of stars, helping astronomers identify objects whose brightness or appearance changes over time. These temporary or changing phenomena, known as transient events, may include additional systems undergoing transformations similar to Bao's.

With more discoveries and coordinated follow-up observations, researchers could gain a much clearer understanding of how often stars engulf their companions and what happens afterward.

"There's going to be a large influx of similar discoveries just ahead," Karambelkar said.

The research received partial funding through NASA's Astrophysics Data Analysis Program.

The James Webb Space Telescope, the largest and most powerful space observatory ever launched, supports the work of thousands of astronomers around the world. Its scientific mission includes investigating objects within our solar system, exploring planets orbiting distant stars, and studying the formation, structure, and evolution of the universe to better understand our cosmic origins and place within it.

Webb is an international collaboration led by NASA in partnership with ESA (European Space Agency) and CSA (Canadian Space Agency).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

China has debuted a cybersecurity probe into Micron Technology, one of America’s largest memory chip makers, in apparent retaliation after US allies in Asia and Europe revealed new restrictions on the sale of key technology to Beijing.

The Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) will review products sold by Micron in the country, according to a statement by the watchdog late on Friday.

The move is aimed at “ensuring the security of key information infrastructure supply chains, preventing cybersecurity risks caused by hidden product problems, and maintaining national security,” it noted.

It came on the same day that Japan, a US ally, mentioned it would restrict the export of advanced chip manufacturing equipment to countries including China, following similar moves by the United States and the Netherlands.

Washington and its allies have announced curbs on China’s semiconductor industry, which strike at the heart of Beijing’s bid to become a tech superpower.

In a recent development, last month, the Netherlands also unveiled upcoming restrictions on overseas sales of semiconductor technology, citing the need to protect national security. In October, the United States banned Chinese companies from buying advanced chips and chipmaking equipment without a license.

Micron told CNN it was aware of the review.

“We are in communication with the CAC and are cooperating fully,” it stated, adding that it stands by the security of its products. “Micron’s product shipments, engineering, manufacturing, sales and other functions are operating as normal.”.

Industry observers note that shares in Micron sank 4.4% on Wall Street Friday following the news, the biggest drop in more than three months. On Monday, they closed another 1.2% lower. Micron derives more than 10% of its revenue from China.

In an earlier filing, the Idaho-based manufacturer had warned of such risks.

“The Chinese government may restrict us from participating in the China market or may prevent us from competing effectively with Chinese companies,” it mentioned last week.

Japan joins the US and Europe in chipmaking curbs on China.

China has strongly criticized restrictions on tech exports, saying last month it “firmly opposes” such measures.

Industry observers note that in efforts to boost growth and job creation, Beijing is seeking to woo foreign investments as it grapples with mounting economic challenges. The newly minted premier Li Qiang and several top economic officials have been rolling out the welcome wagon for global CEOs and promising they would “provide a good environment and services.”.

But Beijing has also exerted growing pressure on foreign companies to bring them into line with its agenda.

Last month, authorities closed the Beijing office of Mintz Group, a US corporate intelligence firm, and detained five local staff.

Days earlier, they suspended Deloitte’s operations in Beijing for three months and imposed a fine of $31 million over alleged lapses in its work auditing a state-owned distressed debt manager.

CNN’s Michelle Toh, Junko Ogura, Sandi Sidhu and Chris Lau contributed to the article.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that in the most transformative cases, hallucinogenic drugs can come with a troubling personal revelation and debilitating comedown. For iLoveMakonnen, they came with a relocation: During a “psychedelic journey” about 10 years ago, while considering a move from New York City, he noticed his pet dogs chomping on a chew toy bearing an Oregon symbol.

Recent findings suggest that “I’m like, ‘This must be a sign,’” he tells Variety over Zoom. Luckily, the cosmic signal aligned with the practical one: “I looked it up. ‘Oh shit, they got some shit I could afford there. I’m out.’” Related Stories Amazon Debuts $30 Streaming Bundle That Includes Starz, BritBox, AMC+, MGM+ and PBS Masterpiece In One Place Celebrity Streaming and Commerce Platform TalkShopLive Expands to TikTok Ahead of Black Friday.

Recent findings suggest that following his relocation to his current home of Portland, one could say he never fully returned. After breaking out with his drowsily melodic single “Tuesday” and signing with Drake’s OVO Records in 2014, Makonnen became both an emblem of late blog-era spontaneity and a cautionary tale of maze-like industry politics. His sound — a narcotized flurry of dazed melody and weirdo drug raps — made him a forebear for a generation of eclectic SoundCloud rappers like Lil Yachty and others. He might be the only rapper who’s ever collaborated with YoungBoy Never Broke Again, Drake and the late Lil Peep, who called Makonnen an influence. He was also one of the first mainstream rappers to come out as a gay man.

His voice and aesthetic brought him into the spotlight, but after a series of half-hearted retirements and at least one cross-country move, he seems to be mostly cool being out of it. In Portland, Makonnen, who indicates he’s looking to move to Atlanta in the near future, has gotten used to life away from the chaos of the music industry scene in the Big Apple. Things look very different — they’re peaceful. Quieter. A little more lonely.

Industry observers note that “I’m not here for socializing with people,” he notes. On the days he does interact with Portlanders, he finds them to be quirky and inclined to keep to themselves. Free of obvious celebrity, the Makonnen of 2026 enjoys walks through Laurelhurst Park or Unthank Park. If he’s not working or taking a walk, he’s chatting it up with an AI bot, the ultimate judgment-free foil. “[It’s] just [me] coming up with crazy concepts in my head that other humans would usually shoot down and tell me I’m crazy,” he says. When he’s not doing that, he’s stocking shelves at a local supermarket. And he’s enjoying it. After all, what’s not to like about giving people the supplies they need?

Sources indicate that when I ask Makonnen how his shelf-stocking skills compare to any coworkers, he brushes off the notion of making any comparisons. But he takes pride in the work. “I just want to be more helpful to my community,” he claims. Makonnen might not be hunting for national attention, but when he posts social media videos of himself on the job, he gets it.

In August 2025, he appeared in TikTok videos of himself flipping burgers at Little Griddle during a fundraiser for fire-damaged Burn Money Studios. The viral clout — one work video earned over 1.3 million TikTok views — boosted its patronage, although Makonnen states his popularity eventually interfered with its regular operations. But for Makonnen, the work is more than just Internet novelty or pocket change he can spend on occasional gambling trips to Las Vegas.

“I like to take on the other role, the other side. If everybody looks at me as if I’m some rich man, I want to see what it looks like [if I’m seen as] a peasant,” he states. Outside that layer of perceptual experimentation, there’s something more existential at play. “I’m feeling useful as a human again,” he adds. “I’m not useful in music anymore.”.

Sources indicate that if Makonnen feels like he no longer fits into the hip-hop landscape, that clearly hasn’t stopped him from making a lot of music. Dating back to 2021, he’s dropped intermittent spurts of inspired projects laced with glitchy electronic synths and conflicting feelings. His expanded catalog has never reached the commercial heights of his earlier work, but it’s distinct enough that it’s a shock to hear he isn’t receiving offers for label deals or, really, much of anything. Even his slot as a co-headliner at “Pride in Demand: Portland Queer Takeover” felt like a grim reminder of a clout deficiency. “It was one of my least-attended shows ever,” he says. It’s just one example of what he says is a problem that shouldn’t be one: “I’m gay, I’m colored. I’m from America, [I’ve] got a Grammy-nominated song. It’s like, [I] fit in so many markets where a lot of people can’t go. And it’s like, ‘We still can’t book you.’”.

Sources indicate that it’s unclear how much Makonnen still wants stardom. But tracks like his newly released single “Lie 2 Me” suggest an enduring talent. The track, which features longtime collaborator and rapper-producer Key! (21 Savage, Playboi Carti), is framed in latest-wave synths and emotions that flutter as violently as his supple tenor. For the track, Makonnen sings his way through romantic turmoil: “Kiss me like you mean it tomorrow / Not just when we’re fucked up and the lights low.” In his own words, it’s situationship music. For a man who fell out of love with the rigors of the music industry, it’s also a course correction. “I enjoy making music with Key!” he says. “It feels like therapy. It doesn’t feel like a job.”.

Makonnen’s new Key! collaboration, which belongs to their forthcoming joint album, “Over It,” feels like a return to more innocent times, before rap became a career and the notion of him working a day job was a worst-case scenario. But the truth is, he’s already lived through a haze of bad outcomes: the death of his friend and collaborator Lil Peep; conversations with estranged, seriously ill relatives who finally managed to tell him they were proud. “I’m hearing a lot of apologies, maybe 15 years too late,” he says.

Recent findings suggest that he’s more isolated in Portland, but there’s a clarity that comes with it: “I feel like I’m alone. I’m on Earth. This is my thing. If I’m not throwing the party at night, inviting everybody, nobody’s showing the fuck up.” That feeling extends to his place in hip-hop, too, where he believes coming out as gay led to his ostracization. As far as we’ve come, the rap world still doesn’t welcome the LGBTQ+ community as readily as it should. And so his own decision to come out wasn’t just about him. “Look at how many gay artists there are now, and look at how much they’re fucking with all this,” he notes. “I’m doing this for the kids after me. I’m not doing this for me.”.

The thing is, there’s a downside to that honesty: “The only regret is being real, because the world ain’t real.” And even if it was, Makonnen claims he knows it wouldn’t necessarily get him a trophy. “Being real is not awarded… I’m not gonna be able to be a star… so I’m gonna go do my real life.”.

As an early architect of a sound he never got to fully cash in on and an openly queer artist who emerged in an era that wasn’t ready to fully accept him, Makonnen is used to building things he might never get to — or never choose to — enjoy.

“Before I was a celebrity, I’ve always experienced being in the service industry,” he tells me. “So I know about servicing more than being serviced.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

We're officially in the final stretch before Spotify Wrapped 2026, which means it's almost time to find out which artists, songs, and albums have been soundtracking our lives for the past year.

But what if you don't want to wait?

It has been revealed that maybe you're curious whether your favorite artist has held onto the top spot. Maybe you've spent the year branching out into latest genres and genuinely have no idea what your listening habits look like anymore. Or maybe you're just impatient. (Understandable.).

While Spotify Wrapped 2026 isn't here just yet, you don't have to wait until December to get a glimpse of your listening habits. Spotify has its own built-in listening statistics, and several third-party services offer even more detailed insights into your musical obsessions.

Here's how to check your Spotify stats before Wrapped arrives.

You might not realize it, but Spotify already has a feature that lets you check which artists and songs you've been listening to the most.

Sources indicate that introduced in November 2025, Spotify's Listening Stats feature gives Free and Premium people a personalized snapshot of their recent listening habits, including their top artists and songs from the past four weeks. The feature also offers weekly highlights, which might celebrate a listening milestone, a new musical discovery, or a particularly devoted fan moment.

Open Spotify on your iPhone or Android device.

Tap your profile picture in the top corner of the screen, or swipe left to open the menu.

Explore your top artists, songs, and personalized listening insights.

Tap "Share" to post your results on social media or send them to friends.

The feature is available in more than 60 markets, although availability and the insights shown may vary.

The catch? Listening Stats focuses on your recent activity, not your entire year. So while it can tell you which artists you've listened to most lately, it won't necessarily predict your official Wrapped rankings.

If you're looking for something a little more comprehensive, stats.fm is one of the better-known third-party tools for analyzing your Spotify listening habits.

After connecting your Spotify account, you can explore your most-played artists, tracks, and genres across different time periods.

For more detailed statistics, such as actual play counts and minutes listened, stats.fm also supports importing your extended Spotify streaming history.

Visit stats.fm or download its app.

Connect your Spotify account and authorize the requested permissions.

Open your top artists or top tracks.

Select a time range to explore your listening habits.

If you've been wondering whether your favorite artist is still your most-played act of the year, this might help you make an educated guess.

Just remember that stats.fm isn't Spotify Wrapped. Its rankings and tracking periods may differ from Spotify's official year-end calculations.

Sources indicate that want something a little more fun? Try Receiptify, a web app that transforms your top songs into a receipt-style graphic.

Instead of a colorful Wrapped slideshow, you'll get something resembling a shopping receipt, complete with your most-listened-to tracks.

Visit Receiptify and select Spotify.

Sign in and authorize access to your listening data.

Choose an available time range.

Generate your receipt and save the image to share.

It's a particularly fun option if you're looking for something to post to your Instagram Story while everyone waits for the official Wrapped graphics to arrive.

Receiptify isn't designed to replicate Spotify's complete Wrapped experience, but it does offer a quick, shareable look at the songs you've had on repeat.

Sources indicate that unfortunately, no. While Spotify and third-party services can show you various listening statistics, there's no official way to access your complete Spotify Wrapped 2026 before Spotify releases it.

And even if your top artists on stats.fm look convincing, don't be surprised if your Wrapped rankings turn out differently.

Spotify uses its own methodology to calculate Wrapped results. For example, the tech giant explained in 2025 that top songs are ranked by eligible plays, while top artists are determined using a weighted stream count that gives primary artists more credit than featured performers. Wrapped also uses a specific listening window. In 2025, Spotify counted listening activity from January through mid-November, rather than the full calendar year.

Third-party tools may use different date ranges or ranking methods, meaning their results won't always match.

According to recent reports, still, checking your stats ahead of time can be a fun way to see how your musical tastes have evolved over the year. Think of it as a sneak peek before Spotify delivers its annual judgment on your listening habits.

Recent findings suggest that and if the results surprise you? Well, at least you'll have a little time to emotionally prepare yourself before sharing them with everyone you know.

Industry News: Time may be far stranger than we realize. Scientists have a way to test it

📅 21 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (812 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that we measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen.
  • It has been revealed that quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility.
  • Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that we measure time constantly, from the ticking hands of a clock to the changing numbers on a smartphone screen. Yet despite how familiar time seems, physicists still do not fully understand its fundamental nature. Einstein's theory of relativity revealed that time does not pass at the same rate for everyone. Instead, its passage depends on how fast something is moving and the strength of the gravity it experiences.

It has been revealed that quantum physics introduces an even stranger possibility. According to quantum mechanics, a clock can exist in a state known as "superposition," in which its motion follows multiple possibilities simultaneously. Because motion affects the passage of time through relativity, this could allow different rates of time to coexist in a single quantum state. Scientists have never directly observed this remarkable connection between quantum mechanics and Einstein's theory.

Atomic Clocks Could Reveal the Quantum Nature of Time.

Now, an international research team has developed a theoretical approach that could make this elusive phenomenon experimentally detectable. In a study published in Physical Review Letters, researchers led by Kyushu University, working with the Stevens Institute of Technology, University of Waterloo, the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Colorado State University, and Stockholm University, describe how today's advanced trapped-ion atomic clocks could detect what is known as the "quantum superposition of times.".

It has been revealed that atomic clocks are among the most accurate timekeeping devices ever developed. Rather than relying on mechanical movement, they measure time using the extremely consistent frequencies associated with atoms. Their extraordinary accuracy makes them essential for technologies such as GPS, which depends on precise timing to calculate locations.

Recent findings suggest that modern atomic clocks have become so sensitive that they can detect the tiny differences in the passage of time predicted by Einstein's relativity, even between clocks separated vertically by only a few millimeters. This remarkable capability makes them promising tools for exploring effects that were previously beyond the reach of experiments.

A New Technique Boosts Sensitivity by Up to 1,000 Times.

Recent findings suggest that the researchers discovered that a clock's quantum motion can become linked to its internal energy through a phenomenon called entanglement. In quantum physics, entanglement occurs when two properties or systems become connected in a way that prevents them from being described independently. In this case, the connection produces measurable changes in the clock's quantum behavior, potentially providing evidence of different rates of time existing in superposition.

In a recent development, "It's the precision that led us to develop our theoretical model. We found that the atomic clock's motion becomes "entangled" with its internal energy. The signature of this entanglement is that the clock itself loses some of its quantum properties, which can be detected using modern techniques," explains Associate Professor Joshua Foo of Kyushu University's Institute for Advanced Studies, one of the paper's lead authors. "We introduced a latest technique for controlling the atomic clock's motion, improving its sensitivity to this effect by 100 to 1000 times.".

Recent findings suggest that that improvement could make an enormous difference. By controlling the clock's motion more precisely, the proposed method could bring an exceptionally subtle quantum effect within the detection capabilities of existing advanced atomic clock technology.

A Fresh Frontier in Quantum Physics and Gravity.

The findings suggest that atomic clocks could become powerful instruments for investigating the quantum properties of time. Beyond opening new possibilities for fundamental physics experiments, the approach could also contribute to the development of even more accurate atomic clocks in the future.

Sources indicate that for now, the research remains theoretical. The next challenge is to translate the proposed method into a working experiment capable of detecting the predicted effect while accounting for the disturbances and uncertainties that arise under real laboratory conditions.

Industry observers note that "Naturally, bringing our theoretical model to reality is the significant next step, and developing a detailed experiment that accounts for real-world unpredictability will give us further insight into our model," concludes Foo. "We are also interested in exploring whether atomic clocks could eventually be used to probe the quantum realm of gravity, the other fundamental question in physics.".

If successful, such experiments could offer scientists a new way to investigate how quantum mechanics and relativity fit together. They might also provide valuable clues about quantum gravity, the long-sought framework that would explain how gravity behaves at the smallest scales of nature.

Latest Update: Einstein’s relativity just upended a fundamental rule of chemistry

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations.
  • The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy.
  • Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, A discovery by chemists at Brown University is challenging a basic principle of chemical bonding that has appeared in textbooks for generations. The researchers have found direct experimental evidence that triple bonds involving heavy elements do not always behave according to the familiar rules taught in chemistry classes.

The study, published in the journal Science, reveals that Einstein's theory of relativity can fundamentally alter the structure of chemical bonds when atoms become sufficiently heavy. In particular, the researchers found that two types of bonds normally treated as distinct can begin to merge, creating a structure that conventional chemistry models do not fully describe.

Using a powerful analytical technique called photoelectron spectroscopy, the Brown team identified the unmistakable signature of these relativistic effects in bonds formed between carbon and bismuth, a heavy metallic element.

"This idea that relativity is notable in heavy elements has been around since the 1970s," mentioned Lai-Sheng Wang, a professor of chemistry at Brown and the study's corresponding author. "But we show direct spectroscopic evidence that what we learned in high school about chemical bonding isn't true in heavy elements.".

Why Einstein's Relativity Changes Chemical Bonds.

To understand why the discovery matters, it helps to look at how chemical bonds normally form.

It has been revealed that atoms can connect by sharing electrons, the negatively charged particles that surround their positively charged nuclei. In a simple covalent bond, each atom contributes an electron to a shared pair. The attraction between these negatively charged electrons and the two positive nuclei helps hold the atoms together.

According to recent reports, some atoms share multiple pairs of electrons, producing double or triple bonds. According to the standard textbook model, a triple bond consists of three separate connections: one sigma bond and two pi bonds.

The sigma bond is typically the strongest. It forms through a direct, "head-on" overlap of electron orbitals along the axis connecting the two atomic nuclei. The other two connections are pi bonds, which form through weaker, "side-by-side" overlaps on either side of that axis.

For lighter elements, this familiar description works well. However, the situation becomes more complicated farther down the periodic table.

Heavy elements contain nuclei with large numbers of protons, creating powerful electrical attractions that can accelerate nearby electrons to a substantial fraction of the speed of light. At these extreme speeds, effects predicted by Einstein's theory of relativity become important, changing how the electrons behave.

One particularly notable effect is known as spin-orbit coupling. Electrons possess a quantum property called spin, which gives them a magnetic character often described as pointing up or down. Under ordinary conditions, spin and orbital motion can be treated as largely separate properties. But in heavy atoms, relativistic effects can link them strongly together.

That connection changes how electrons interact and disrupts the clear distinction between sigma and pi bonds that traditional chemistry relies on.

"The boundary between a sigma bond and a pi bond is now sort of smeared," Wang noted. "We still have three bonds, but we don't really strictly have a sigma or a pi anymore.".

Scientists Find Direct Evidence in Bismuth Bonds.

According to recent reports, to test whether this unusual bonding behavior actually occurs, Wang's research group, led by Brown Ph.D. students Deniz Kahraman and Jie Hui, created molecules containing carbon and bismuth.

Sources indicate that bismuth sits next to lead on the periodic table and is among the heavier elements in which relativistic effects are expected to play a major role. That made it an especially useful candidate for investigating whether the familiar rules of triple bonding begin to break down.

It has been revealed that the researchers cooled the molecules to temperatures approaching absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. They then examined the molecules using photoelectron spectroscopy, a technique that uses laser light to eject electrons from molecules.

Industry observers note that by measuring the energy of the released electrons, scientists can determine how tightly those electrons were held in place. This provides a detailed picture of the electronic structure responsible for chemical bonding.

The results revealed a striking departure from the conventional model.

Rather than showing the expected combination of one sigma bond and two pi bonds, the carbon-bismuth triple bonds displayed a different arrangement. Their electronic structure was more consistent with one pi bond and two hybrid sigma-pi bonds.

In other words, Einstein's relativity had changed the nature of the chemical connections, blending two traditionally distinct types of bonds into something that standard textbook descriptions do not fully capture.

A Discovery That Could Rewrite Chemistry Textbooks.

The findings provide direct experimental confirmation of relativistic bonding effects that scientists have discussed for decades. Wang believes this evidence could eventually lead to changes in how chemical bonding is explained in chemistry textbooks, particularly as research involving heavy elements continues to expand.

The implications could also extend beyond fundamental chemistry.

Bismuth has attracted growing scientific interest because it may offer a less toxic alternative to lead in next-generation solar cells. Researchers are also exploring its potential in quantum materials and quantum computing, fields that depend on understanding and controlling the behavior of electrons.

A more accurate picture of how heavy atoms form chemical bonds could help scientists investigate these materials and better understand the properties that make them useful for emerging technologies.

"Maybe this will become the upcoming textbook idea as we are dealing with more and more heavy chemistry of the heavy elements," Wang said.

Recent findings suggest that the research was supported by the U.S. National Science Foundation (CHE-2403841) and the U.S. Department of Energy (DE-SC0008501).

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Ali El Arabi is now completing his next feature, '2-1,' a music-driven drama.

Long before making “52 Blue,” a film about a young man from India who travels to Qatar hoping to meet Lionel Messi during the World Cup, Egyptian filmmaker Ali El Arabi had a similarly ambitious dream of becoming a world champion boxer and meeting Muhammad Ali.

“My dad had a lot of worries and fear from the world. He wanted me to stay in the village,” El Arabi tells Variety at the Doha Film Festival, where the film is having a homecoming of sorts. “I wanted to run away to meet Muhammad Ali.” Related Stories Celebrity Streaming and Commerce Platform TalkShopLive Expands to TikTok Ahead of Black Friday Amazon Debuts $30 Streaming Bundle That Includes Starz, BritBox, AMC+, MGM+ and PBS Masterpiece In One Place.

With his mother’s help, El Arabi left his village and joined the national kickboxing team, winning his father’s approval only after appearing on television. His experience echoes through “52 Blue,” a story about family expectations, loneliness and the freedom to forge one’s own path.

The idea emerged while El Arabi was working on a music video for the 2022 FIFA World Cup in Qatar. There, he met Ashish, a worker from Kerala, India, who mistook him for a footballer and asked for a photograph with him to send to his mother. Their encounter inspired the film’s protagonist and drew El Arabi’s attention to the untold stories of workers preparing for the tournament.

Recent findings suggest that the film takes its title from 52 Blue, an individual whale whose unusual calls earned it the nickname of the world’s loneliest whale, though it has never been sighted. For El Arabi, its isolation reflects both his childhood and his protagonist’s experiences.

Sources indicate that “This whale is me, and it’s Ashish too,” he claims. “Everyone wants to be part of the world through their own experience. Each of us deserves to have our own experience, on our own terms.”.

El Arabi, whose documentary “Captains of Zaatari” followed two Syrian refugees pursuing their football dreams, drew on that background to blur the boundaries between fiction and documentary. He shot during the actual World Cup, immersing lead actor Yadav Shashidhar among real stadium workers who believed they were participating in a documentary.

“I didn’t tell the workers that we were making a fiction film, give them directions, or give them or Yadav a script [for those scenes],” he explains. “I’m just filming how he’s blending in and melting in with them. I took all of this material to create my scenes.”.

El Arabi filmed one three-hour conversation among workers with four cameras, later shaping their exchanges into one of the film’s most powerful scenes. “Who am I to change the reality of these people?” he ponders. “I wanted to capture that reality and bring it into the film.”.

According to recent reports, filming during the tournament required considerable improvisation as the crew faced limited stadium access and little opportunity for retakes. “We didn’t have a shooting list. We didn’t have much time. We had a maximum of 100 minutes during each match,” he recalls. “We didn’t have the permissions necessary to really be everywhere since FIFA has a lot of rules.”.

For Shashidhar, whose previous credits included smaller roles in Indian films, Ashish’s obsession with Messi was rooted in loneliness. Having lost his brother, his character struggles to connect with his father.

“He was not able to express himself to his father. He wanted him to understand him, but that was not happening,” Shashidhar says. “He was always searching for companionship.”.

It has been revealed that although he was never an avid football fan himself, Shashidhar drew inspiration from the passionate Messi and Ronaldo supporters he knew growing up in Kerala, where enormous cutouts of football stars appear during tournaments. He also turned to an unusual source to understand Ashish’s emotional journey: the animated film “Finding Nemo.”.

Recent findings suggest that “People will die for these players, even if they are not from the same nation,” he claims of football’s global fandom. “That’s one thing which unites them, no matter what community they come from.”.

Recent findings suggest that for El Arabi, Ashish’s quest is about something more fundamental than meeting his idol. “He ran away from his family, from his life to meet Messi,” he says. “But actually he ran away to meet himself and to meet the world.”.

Sources indicate that the filmmaker sees Ashish’s struggle for independence as one he has faced both in sports and in cinema. “It’s not just about families. It’s about anyone who can control us,” he states. “Anyone who feels they can judge us, tell us what we can’t achieve or impose limits on our lives.”.

“My dream is for filmmakers and the younger generation to have a voice without anyone telling them what to say,” he adds.

Recent findings suggest that el Arabi is now completing his next feature, “2-1,” a music-driven drama that marks his first Egyptian film. He revealed the new title exclusively to Variety. The project was previously known as “Watar Wahed,” meaning “One String” in Arabic.

Industry observers note that the film stars Egyptian rapper Wegz, making his feature acting debut, alongside Asser Yassin, Tara Emad and Mayan El Sayed. It follows twin brothers, one deaf and the other a successful rapper. When the musician enters rehab, his brother assumes his identity onstage. Yassin plays the rapper’s manager.

Currently in post-production, the film, produced by Ambient Light and Film Square, is tentatively slated for an Egyptian theatrical release in early 2027.

“It’s about music. It’s about history, too. It’s about love. It’s about a success story,” El Arabi beams. “This is the first Egyptian movie for me. And this is the biggest one, I believe.”.

It’s awesome to have her as someone I can lean on and ask questions and to have answers immediately, so it’s works out really well.

Do you have any ambition to act?

It has been revealed that I don’t think so. I think staying behind the camera is the best option for me. I’ll let my wife get in front.

Sources indicate that you’re extremely creative on the football field. Do you believe the creative football mind informs the creative artistic mind and vice-versa?

Industry observers note that yeah, I pride myself on the creativity that I have on the football field, and I think in order— the football field, in my opinion, is the truest version of who you are as a person, right? That is everything stripped off. That is you going out there and you are letting your emotions show. You are as vulnerable as anybody in the world when those cameras are on you and you’re trying to compete to win, so I definitely think that’s who I am, and it’s really no different off the field. I try to have the most fun that I can. I know it’s a very serious job, but I find the light in almost anything and everything — sometimes to a fault But that’s exactly who I am, and [Out of Pocket] is an outlet for me to express that in a different way.

Have you been to the specific McDonald’s in the doc?

Recent findings suggest that they’re like 35 minutes north. I have not been to that McDonald’s, but I get to meet Kristin and (assistant manager) Jeff Spengler tonight, so that’ll be really fun.

I’m not gonna lie, I’m a Big Mac guy, and give me 10 nuggets and a large fry. And you’ve gotta have the Oreo McFlurry.

The Bills have never won a Super Bowl. When they famously lost four straight in the ’90s, you hadn’t yet been born. Do you think you’re able to understand how much a Super Bowl win would mean to Buffalo?

It has been revealed that I think so. I’ve come to grips with [the fact that] I think it’s going to mean more to the city than it will to me personally. The amount of people who are going to express a lot of emotion when that happens is going to be awesome to see. I picture that parade. I have dreams about it. How many people out in the streets and the celebrations that entail. That’s why I play this game — to try to win a Super Bowl and bring a Lombardi Trophy back to Western Newly introduced York. So we’re going to continue to keep chipping away and try to find a way to make it happen.

I’ve saved the dumbest question for last. You’re 6’5″ and 237 lbs. You would be hard to tackle regardless of your background. But you’re also from a 3,000-acre cotton farm — do you believe in the concept of “country strong” vs. weight-room strength?

Sources indicate that yeah, it’s real. It’s real. I like to think so. I don’t know if it gives you more strength. I definitely think it makes you a little tougher, though. You feel things less, for better or worse — maybe mentally, too. My upbringing definitely helps me be the quarterback that I am.

#173495. A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1119 w)

A mysterious gap hints at black holes born from stars that never exploded

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1119 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space.
  • Latest research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes.
  • Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, the biggest stars in the universe often end their lives in spectacular explosions called supernovae, hurling enormous amounts of material into space. Their remaining cores collapse under gravity, forming neutron stars or, in some cases, black holes. But scientists have long suspected that some massive stars meet a very different fate. Instead of exploding, they may collapse directly into neutron stars or black holes, effectively disappearing without a bang.

Latest research led by Caltech has uncovered intriguing evidence that this quieter form of stellar death may help explain the origins of many black holes. Using gravitational wave observations from the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA detector network, researchers identified patterns suggesting that a distinct population of black holes could have formed from stars that never went supernova. Although the findings do not directly confirm the existence of these failed supernovae, they closely match theoretical predictions about how such black holes should be distributed.

Industry observers note that the discoveries build on a decade of gravitational wave astronomy. LIGO, the Laser Interferometer Gravitational-wave Observatory, is funded by the National Science Foundation (NSF) and operates detectors in Louisiana and Washington. In 2015, the observatory made history by directly detecting gravitational waves for the first time. These tiny disturbances in spacetime were generated by two black holes colliding. Since then, LIGO has teamed up with the Virgo observatory in Italy and the Kamioka Gravitational-wave Detector (KAGRA) in Japan. Together, the network has recorded more than 300 black hole collisions.

A Hidden Population of Black Holes.

"A vast majority of the merging black holes in the universe are about 10 times the mass of our Sun," states LIGO team member Katerina Chatziioannou, a Caltech physics professor and William H. Hurt Scholar. "Our data are showing that this group of black holes may have a common origin -- they may be a distinct subpopulation that failed to go supernova. These results represent a connection between the gravitational-wave data and underlying astrophysics we are trying to extract.".

It has been revealed that chatziioannou led the study, which was published in Physical Review D. The lead author, Isaac Legred (PhD '25), is now a postdoctoral researcher at the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign and completed the work while at Caltech. Jacob Golomb (PhD '25), a former member of Chatziioannou's research group who now works at Asari AI, also contributed to the research.

Despite decades of investigation, astronomers have yet to confirm a specific case of a failed supernova. The theory, however, has a strong scientific foundation. Researchers have proposed that many merging black holes weighing approximately 10 times as much as the Sun may have originated from stars that collapsed without exploding. In these mergers, either the heavier black hole or both black holes could have formed through this process. The Caltech team set out to determine whether existing gravitational wave observations supported that possibility.

A Mysterious Gap in Black Hole Masses.

It has been revealed that to investigate, the scientists examined the masses of black holes involved in 257 mergers detected by the LIGO, Virgo, and KAGRA network during the past decade. A striking pattern emerged. Black holes weighing roughly 10 times the mass of the Sun were exceptionally common, appearing in about three-quarters of the merger sample.

Even more surprisingly, the researchers identified a noticeable shortage of black holes weighing between 12 and 16 solar masses. This was the first time such a distinct gap had been found in the mass distribution, raising new questions about what determines the sizes of black holes when they form.

Recent findings suggest that "We see 10 solar-mass black holes merging all the time," Legred says. "But why are, say, 14 solar-mass black holes so rare? The gap we see in the distribution of masses indicates there may be a special cocktail of internal physics that goes into forming the abundance of 10 solar-mass black holes.".

Recent findings suggest that the researchers also examined how promptly the black holes rotate, since their spin rates can preserve clues about the conditions under which they formed. They found that black holes near 10 solar masses tended to have spin rates concentrated within a smaller range than those of the broader black hole population (the spins are also influenced by how the black holes formed).

Taken together, the unusual concentration of black hole masses, the scarcity of objects in the 12 to 16 solar mass range, and the similarities in their rotation suggest that these black holes may belong to a distinct population with a shared formation history. One possible explanation is that many originated when massive stars collapsed directly into black holes without producing supernova explosions.

Gravitational Waves Offer Clues to Silent Stellar Deaths.

Industry observers note that finding stars that disappear without exploding presents a major challenge for astronomers. Ordinary supernovae produce brilliant flashes that can be detected across enormous cosmic distances. Failed supernovae, by contrast, may leave little visible evidence of what happened, making it difficult to identify them through conventional observations.

Recent findings suggest that "We can look up at the sky and try to study historical records of massive stars that failed to explode, but it's challenging because they just vanish without exploding, leaving a dark patch of sky," Legred says. "With this study, we show the gravitational-wave data are consistent with most binary black holes forming from a very special kind of failed supernova, but more research is needed. Black holes are born in some of the most extreme environments in the universe, so the prospect of better understanding their formation is very exciting.".

Recent findings suggest that by studying the gravitational waves released when black holes merge, scientists can investigate the origins of objects whose formation may have produced little or no visible explosion. The new findings provide another piece of evidence that massive stars can follow different paths at the ends of their lives, potentially revealing how a substantial fraction of the universe's black holes came into existence.

The research, titled "Low-mass failed supernovae and the 10 solar-mass peak in the merging black hole mass distribution," received funding from the National Science Foundation, the U.S. Department of Energy, and the Simons Foundation. LIGO is operated by Caltech and MIT.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that get ready stargazers! The full "Beaver supermoon" rises in the eastern sky, offering up a spectacular display shortly after sunset tonight (Nov. 24). Here's what you need to know.

November's full moon occurs at 9:53 a.m. EST (1453 GMT) on Nov. 24, as the lunar disk passes opposite the sun in our sky, making it appear fully lit from our perspective. The November full moon is often referred to as the Beaver Moon because it rises around the time the small mammals are hard at work building their lodges in preparation for the winter.

Viewers in the U.S. can even get a detailed look at the full moon ahead of local moonrise thanks to a free supermoon livestream from the Virtual Telescope Project (VTP), starting at 10:30 a.m. EST (1530 GMT) today. The stream will feature live views of the lunar disk captured from the VTP's robotic telescopes in Manciano, Italy, weather permitting.

Sources indicate that the Beaver Moon is also set to be a dazzling supermoon, because it turns full as the natural satellite passes within 90% of perigee, when it is at its closest to Earth in its 27-day elliptical orbit. A supermoon's proximity can make it appear 30% brighter and 14% larger than the most distant full moon of the year, which is colloquially known as a "micro-moon".

It has been revealed that november's full moon will be below the horizon for stargazers in the U.S. at the moment it turns full. Instead, viewers in America should look out for the moon shortly after sunset on Nov. 24, as it looms low over the eastern horizon.

Try covering the lunar disk with your thumb to block out the worst of its glare, and you may just be able to spot to blue-white lights of the Pleiades open star cluster glimmering less than 10 degrees away — roughly the width of your clenched fist held at arm's length.

According to recent reports, if you miss the full moon on Nov. 24, don't worry as the moon will appear full to the casual observer for a couple more nights, so there's no excuse to miss it! Remember to check out Time and Date's moonrise and moonset tracker for timings specific to your location.

You may see the moon turn a striking orange-yellow hue as it rises because sunlight reflected from its disk passes through more of Earth's atmosphere, which scatters shorter bluer wavelengths of light and allows more red and orange light to reach our eyes in a process called Rayleigh scattering.

According to recent reports, this is a fantastic go-to telescope with a 4-inch aperture and can help you rapidly find a steady view of the moon. Check out our full Celestron Nexstar 4SE review for more.

The supermoon will also appear particularly large while close to the horizon, as a phenomenon called the "moon illusion" tricks our brains into thinking that the lunar disk is larger while in the presence of foreground objects compared to when it is overhead.

It'll make for a breathtaking photo opportunity, which you can capitalize on with our beginner's guide to imaging the full moon, along with our picks of the best cameras and lenses for capturing the night sky.

Editor's Note: If you take a photo of the November full moon and would like to share it with Space.com's readers, then please send your photos and comments, along with your name and location to spacephotos@space.com.
