  • Industry observers note that two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed.
  • Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On the morning of May 31, 2025, Shirley Bekker made an impulsive decision. The then 29-year-old doctor living in London finally pulled the trigger on plane tickets to visit Foshan, in southern China, for a flight later that same day.

Industry observers note that two months prior, Bekker had little knowledge of the city of 9 million; she had no idea what hotel to stay at or where to go once she landed. But Bekker was convinced that six days in Foshan to furnish her apartment—and possibly having all of the furniture shipped back to London—would still be cheaper than getting everything at home. With over 100,000 followers on social media, she also later turned her adventure into content, detailing her finds and their cost.

Bekker was in the process of buying her dream one-bedroom apartment in East London and spent weeks obsessively watching home renovation videos on TikTok. “When I saw that things like a sofa cost thousands of pounds, I was like, ‘OK, I’m convinced now that I’ll probably do something drastic to not have to pay that much,’” she notes. Her social media algorithm was already feeding her a radical solution. “Made in China, shit quality?” a Chinese furniture seller said in videos on Bekker’s TikTok feed. “Grass sofa? Our factory has mass-produced it; UFO table? Our factory has mass-produced it.” Soon, Bekker says, her “entire timeline became Foshan, Foshan, Foshan.” She learned all about China’s furniture capital, which each year exports nearly $10 billion worth of couches and beds and bathroom vanities, and everything else you could possibly need for your home.

In a recent development, bekker is just one of a growing number of people around the world who order furniture directly from factories in Foshan. By either flying to the city—or through WhatsApp, TikTok, AliExpress, or Alibaba—buyers can commission made-to-order pieces. And most importantly, they can purchase dupes.

In 2025, Shirley Bekker flew to China to buy furniture, hoping that even with shipping the cost would be lower than shopping in London.

In a recent development, duplicates were once primarily the domain of fashion and beauty, but consumers are now seeking out knockoffs of luxury designer furniture that promise the same quality as the original at a much lower cost—even after international shipping rates and tariffs. During the week of April 13, 2025, the number of videos urging Americans to buy directly from Chinese factories soared 250 percent. Tens of thousands of videos had been posted under hashtags like #ChineseFactory, and many of them were about furniture pieces. Some videos garnered millions of views and included contacts of Chinese sellers in the comments.

@gabwithmeg, a working mom in California, claims on TikTok that she saved at least $100,000 by furnishing her entire house directly from China. “It is all Restoration Hardware and Arhaus-style furniture, and I’m going to tell you exactly how I did it,” she promised her followers in January. @gabwithmeg’s post received over 65,000 likes, and the comments are filled with users clamoring to opt out of the traditional furniture market, if not bragging about having already done so.

Together, they represent a turning tide in furniture shopping for Westerners. If people can buy a couch that looks exactly like the famous Togo for $200 on AliExpress, why would they pay $4,800 for one from Design Within Reach? Sure, Ligne Roset is a legendary brand, famously crafting all its furniture near the French Alps, made by trained artisans using an almost entirely manual process. But not everyone cares about history, owning an original, or the ethics of intellectual property in design. In fact, some furniture buyers, including Bekker, aren’t even aware that some pieces they covet are copies. Bekker feels that designer furniture is more expensive because of the brand name, not necessarily the quality. “Sorry to say, for me, it’s a bit bullshit,” she indicates. “I’m really not one to buy into the idea that the name of the brand makes it worth the price.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re seeing the beginnings of a revolt against the brandification of everything,” indicates Christopher Sprigman, a law professor at New York University who has studied the knockoff economy. As a consumer, Sprigman expects brands to offer good and consistent quality, but there is a perception that “there’s no real quality control, there’s no real integrity, it’s basically just advertising and driving up costs, creating demand, creating desire without any real substantial benefit that the consumer can feel or taste or see,” Sprigman says.

The videos Bekker saw never explicitly remarked how much the furniture in Foshan would cost, but she was confident it would be far less than at the posh showrooms in London. Despite not speaking Chinese, she roamed around the furniture markets in Foshan’s warm and humid air. By the end of the trip, she had furnished her entire apartment for around £7,000 (about $9,200). Everything would go in a 20-foot container, embark from Guangzhou on a freight ship, and arrive at an English port more than two months later. Bekker’s videos attracted millions of views, and fans swarmed to the comments with the same refrain: “I have never been so influenced to go to China.”.

Four million people from over 150 countries visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture.

Everyone who goes to Foshan for furniture makes sure to go to the Louvre.

Recent findings suggest that in the central part of Foshan, the Louvre claims to be one of the largest furniture shopping malls in China, and likely the whole world. At over 4 million square feet, it’s bigger than its namesake in France, which is the largest museum in the world; 4 million people from over 150 countries and regions visit Foshan’s Louvre every year to shop for furniture. Past the facade—which looks like an outdated convention center with blue-tinted windows and rows of country flags above the entrance—is an opulent atrium with marble columns and gilded moldings.

Industry observers note that the complex was designed to be part of a tourist experience package, with official certification from the Chinese tourism bureau. There’s a shuttle bus from the nearest international airport and a five-star Sofitel hotel for guests. In addition to tourists from the US and Europe, there are ever more shoppers, architects, and traders from the Middle East, Africa, Russia, Central Asia, and South Asia.

In a recent development, the Louvre contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones, so there’s something for everyone. As many of these brands construct their furniture in Foshan, it’s the ideal place for a showroom. Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics here, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “new Chinese,” and wabi-sabi. In most places, photography is strictly prohibited to “protect original designs.”.

Industry observers note that but the Louvre is often just a shopper’s first destination. “Foshan is not actually one furniture market. It’s a district, it’s a city, it’s an ecosystem,” claims Claudia Hofmeister, an Australia-based furniture sourcing agent who has helped clients from around the world buy furniture from Foshan; she has personally traveled there at least six times. While the Louvre is the pinnacle of luxury furniture shopping, Foshan also offers other mid-tier wholesale businesses that are 100 percent Chinese, plus lower-end furniture brands that Hofmeister says she won’t touch. “And there’s a whole lot of other models like massive supercenters just dedicated to lighting, tiles, and building supplies,” she says.

Industry observers note that for many travelers, the real shopping doesn’t happen there. The dupe factories, along with home construction and decor manufacturers, are a few miles away in Longjiang. Longjiang is known as the hub of furniture manufacturing, where you can find everything from fabrics to timber to metal parts. Its streets are lined with miles of furniture shops and nothing else. The town has its own exhibition center, but it stands in stark contrast to the opulent tourism spectacle at the Louvre.

The Louvre International Furniture Exhibition Center contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Industry observers note that every March and August, Longjiang hosts its own furniture fair, which attracts small manufacturers, dealers, and domestic buyers from other parts of China. The furniture brands in the district care less about original design and are sometimes explicit about where they draw inspiration. On the facade of a showroom building next to the exhibition center, a billboard-sized banner advertises a “Lawrence sofa,” a popular 2017 design by the famous Italian brand Minotti that can sell for over $10,000. In their booths, some sellers display portraits of a white “art director,” an Italian flag, or plaster sculptures.

Even for Chinese people, the idea of traveling to Foshan to buy furniture instead of placing orders from home is relatively latest. As China’s real estate economy slowed over the past decade, the traditional business model of licensed furniture distribution struggled. Factories now have to contend with tariffs and competition from countries where labor can be cheaper. Sourcing companies position themselves to factories as a more direct connection to consumers. Even though buyers pay to travel, they can save “30 percent to 50 percent” while still gaining access to new designs and high-quality products, says Lin Fangfang, the founder and chairman of Yueanju, one of the earliest and most influential B2C furniture sourcing agents in China.

In a recent development, yueanju, which was founded in 2016, says it has worked closely with the local government to develop the “travel to Foshan” marketing strategy. On the radio nationwide, ads hype shopping for furniture in Foshan, with organized pickups from train stations and airports, as well as customized factory tours based on specific needs and budget. A typical three-day trip costs as little as $170 per person. Agents take care of everything and even provide a cafeteria and nap area with recliners in Yueanju’s office building in Longjiang. “Even though [Longjiang is] only one bridge away, they just won’t come here because they don’t know about us,” Lin says. “[Now], we can accommodate over 200 visitors with no problem on this floor.”.

According to recent reports, services like what Yueanju offers quickly exploded in popularity, bringing a steady flow of consumers to what had previously been a business-to-business manufacturing hub. They are now working with clients from countries including the US, Russia, Saudi Arabia, and Australia. In March, during Ramadan, the company hosted a group from Saudi Arabia. “They are royals, so their homes are pretty big,” Lin indicates. The company customized the shopping experience based on their fasting needs, only going out after 3 pm every day to preserve energy.

According to recent reports, the modern history of furniture in Foshan started with a dupe. As the lore goes, in the 1970s a man named Li Jungang working at a carpentry factory got his hands on a couch from nearby Hong Kong, then a British colony. While upholstered furniture took off in Europe in the 17th century, traditional chairs in China were still made of hardwood and had no built-in cushioning. By the 1970s in Hong Kong, upholstered, Western-style couches were all the rage. Li cut open the couch, studied interior construction, and is said to have built what is considered the first-ever upholstered sofa in China. Similar stories citing the origin of Foshan’s relatively short history in modern furniture manufacturing are now proudly recorded in local history books, displayed in furniture showrooms, and retold by every entrepreneur in the city.

The Louvre in Foshan contains showrooms for over 2,000 Chinese brands and 400 European ones.

Italian minimalism is one of the most visible aesthetics at the Louvre, but you’ll also find styles like Russian imperial, “new Chinese,” and wabi-sabi.

Industry observers note that the rest of the story tracks the rise of manufacturing in China. As the government started embracing the market economy in the late 1970s, China became the locus of offshore manufacturing for the rest of the world. Foshan’s voracious entrepreneurs and artisans saw an opportunity to remake the city—which until then was known more for kung fu and local cuisine—into a manufacturing powerhouse. The city became known for factories that specialized in building materials, home appliances, and furniture. Foshan’s home goods industry grew to include over 7,000 businesses that account for at least one-fifth of the furniture market in China. In 2025, Foshan exported $2.65 billion worth of furniture alone. “If you have a home, you have something made in Foshan,” says the promotional slogan and industry alliance rolled out by the local government in 2022.

Industry observers note that as the city became a furniture juggernaut, it developed an obsession with Italy and, more specifically, Milan, the capital of 20th-century interior design. At Salone del Mobile, the internationally renowned annual furniture fair showcasing some of the most innovative designs in the world, Foshan factory manufacturers study the latest luxury designs from Italian brands. A smaller number of companies bring their own products to the fair, and local furniture leaders also visit to help promote government collaborations between Foshan and Milan. In 2011, a Chinese newspaper reported that during that year’s furniture fair, Fendi Casa refused to admit Chinese visitors to its showroom. (Salone del Mobile did not respond to a request for comment.).

Recent findings suggest that some Foshan furniture makers do copy designs from Salone, and they do it fast. The 2026 fair ended on April 26; by May 11, Foshan furniture factories were posting on Chinese social media about mass-producing the Anywhere sofa by Edra, one of the breakout products of the year. “The first domestic upcoming Anywhere sofa is here,” says a Chinese woman in a brightly lit showroom, walking past a sofa that looks identical to the original, on Chinese social media platform Rednote. The account, under the name HY Casa, says it’s a source factory in Foshan that specializes in “high-end Italian minimal made-to-order 1:1 furniture dupes.”.

It has been revealed that to create a truly convincing replica, snapping a few photos in Milan is not enough. Wang Xunyong is the owner of EIBA, a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end dupes of Minotti sofas by ordering the original, shipping it back to Foshan, and taking it apart to study its internal structure, just like Li did in the ’70s.

A stack of pocket springs at the EIBA factory.

EIBA is a furniture brand in Foshan that produces high-end sofa dupes.

Before the success of EIBA, Wang had a series of failed ventures—restaurants and several other furnishing-related businesses. Eventually, he arrived at a decision: “Instead of doing a hundred mediocre things, it’s better to take one thing to the extreme,” he states in a video posted on his social media account. In 2023, he founded his current company with a small workshop model, leveraging his past experience in the furniture business. This time, it worked.

Recent findings suggest that wang’s factory in Longjiang occupies the fourth floor of a pristine white industrial building, where a polished lobby opens into a modest showroom/workshop. Several rows of finished sofas sit near the entrance beneath ceiling spotlights. Wang has a makeshift office area that he shares with his sales staff. Every so often, a Bluetooth speaker linked to his phone announces in a flat robotic voice that someone has made a furniture order online. On the workshop floor, five or six women cut and sew sofa fabric, while several men shape foam, spray adhesive, and stretch upholstery over frames.

Wang has never been to Italy. His understanding of Italian design comes from sofas dismantled inside his factory. The first time Wang cut open an Italian-made sofa, he was struck by its complexity. It wasn’t just layers of materials stacked together, but rather a system with different densities, cutting methods, and structural logic working in harmony. He compares the sofa manufacturing process to making a cake: You can standardize the baking process by using a mold, but a complex curve would sometimes require human hands. For a long time, Wang states, many factories focused only on replicating the look of luxury couches. The proportions and silhouettes of the sofas were similar to the originals, but the internal structure was oversimplified. But that misses the essence of what makes a piece of furniture great.

Lin Qi, a factory worker, cuts paper patterns.

Zeng Xiaofeng, a factory worker, cutting fabric.

This path isn’t cheap. Purchasing original pieces requires significant investment, often eight to 10 times the price of the dupes his factory produces. Once the model is thoroughly studied, efficiency improves. Today, Wang says, his team can complete the reproduction of a fresh design within 45 days. This methodology has allowed his factory to reach annual sales of 20 million yuan (about $3 million). Unlike Minotti, which makes almost every piece of its custom furniture in Meda, Italy, Chinese factories can count on much lower costs for labor and manufacturing.

To outsiders, Wang’s work is ethically dubious, but he is unapologetic. “What we’re trying to do is copy it first and surpass it later,” he says. “Many people look down on copying others, but we ignore those noises. First, we learn their details and craftsmanship. Once you have the financial strength and vision, you’ll be much better equipped to do your own thing.”.

In his view, as long as a product does not carry the original brand’s logo, it cannot be considered “counterfeit and substandard.” On a more practical level, he has developed strategies to reduce legal risk. Based on his understanding of regulations, Wang claims, a piece is legally distinct if there are “seven points of difference,” even if that’s as minor as changing a board’s thickness from 3 centimeters to 2.9.

Wang’s rule of seven is a common belief among Chinese manufacturers, but it’s more folklore than law, states Morgan Pietz, managing partner at the Los Angeles office of Merchant & Gould, who has represented both sides of furniture IP lawsuits. “At least under US law, there’s no rule that if you make seven changes, you are good to go,” he says.

It has been revealed that but it is difficult to legally claim that someone has knocked off a furniture design, lawyers say. In the US, most plaintiffs in the furniture industry need to go down one of two routes: Either they register patents for each of their products, or they need to demonstrate that a layperson would be able to discern the product’s origin. Both are difficult hurdles to clear. Design patents can cost around $5,000, including attorney costs and a filing fee for one product, and they only last 15 years; to make a “trade dress” claim, a furniture company needs to show that its consumers recognize the design as being from a specific source. In most cases, furniture designs don’t rise to this level of scrutiny. And no matter which route one chooses, bringing the claim to court and enforcing it could cost millions of dollars.

Industry observers note that sometimes there can even be a correlation between the popularity of dupes and the sales of originals, Sprigman states. When studying the luxury fashion knockoff industry in China, he found that buyers of counterfeit handbags can often move on to purchasing the genuine product once they become wealthier. “For some people, you could view dupes as a gateway drug to the traditional thing,” he says.

Industry observers note that to Wang, the production of dupes is not only a furniture industry phenomenon but also indicative of how capitalism in China works more broadly. “Many of our industries started from scratch. If you want results as fast as possible, you have to learn from abroad first. Whether it’s equipment, aircraft, artillery, or high-speed rail, haven’t we always followed this same path?”.

International clients select materials at the EIBA furniture factory in Foshan, China.

Still, creating dupes is not a business that can scale infinitely. In Wang’s view, the market for copies has become oversaturated, and competitive price wars are eating into profit margins. Foshan brands are now pivoting to original designs, not only out of ethical concerns but also due to market pressure. One day, when he has enough financial capital and experience, he hopes to develop his own designs. And only then will he consider actually traveling to Italy. Not to copy their furniture, but to experience Italian culture and find inspiration.

“You need to truly immerse yourself in that environment to feel what high-end Italian design is really about” he says.

Almost everything in Nikki Brooks’ fresh house came from China, which is how she got the nickname “Container Girl.” Brooks, a TikTok influencer in Texas who finds “affordable fashion” for her followers, started looking for furniture for a new home in 2024. In the past two years, she has bought windows, doors, stone countertops, tiles, beds, sofas, and even a golf cart from Chinese manufacturers, enough to fill four shipping containers.

In a recent development, in addition to her 150,000 followers across TikTok, Instagram, and Facebook, Brooks organized a private Facebook group where over 25,000 members discuss how to source “high-quality, cost-effective materials from overseas—especially China.” In the group, people ask each other how to import, while others share photos of their containers arriving in the US or their beautiful homes stuffed with fresh purchases. Through affiliate marketing, Brooks also gets commissions from “some” products she recommends, according to her personal website.

“We’ve seen a whole crop of dupe influencers pop up, whose livelihoods are based on helping their audiences find the best deals,” says Sky Canaves, an ecommerce analyst at Emarketer, who spent over a decade reporting on China. According to Canaves, beauty and fashion influencers can take a 10 to 15 percent commission from the sales they encourage; in furniture, which is purchased less frequently, the rate can be around 5 percent, but the cost per item is higher.

While in Foshan, Bekker bought everything she needed for her new apartment.

She decided to shop room by room.

A fresh generation of consumers—who came of age with Shein, Temu, and Amazon—consult TikTok or Pinterest instead of design magazines and often buy things directly through these apps. They rarely go to stores in person, if at all, and value affordability over virality. (See the Walmart Birkins, fake AirPods Max, Temu celebrity look-alikes, and everything else that’s been duped.).

“I don’t love the term ‘dupe.’ It sounds awfully cute for something that is essentially buying a knockoff, or a counterfeit, or a theft,” indicates Coleman Gutshall, the vice president of strategic operations at Bernhardt Design, which develops high-end furniture with designers. From his perspective, an original piece of furniture is more expensive not because of an outrageous margin; Gutshall says his company pays fair wages for over 1,500 employees in North Carolina and works with up-and-coming designers. Many iconic pieces that are duped today were conceived of by innovative designers 50 or 100 years ago, he says, “and in order to keep that continuing, you’ve got to have this constant pipeline of designers. If they can’t make a living through loyalty and through designing, then their talent is going to waste.”.

Industry observers note that but not everyone in the design industry is anti-dupe. “There is no way I could ever afford an original, new Togo sofa,” notes Lauren Sinclair, an architect in New York. (A real three-seat Togo—the iconic foam-filled modular couch designed by French industrial designer Michel Ducaroy in 1973 and still handmade in France by artisans—sells for about $10,000 today.) In 2022, Sinclair paid a Chinese factory $200, plus another $700 for shipping, to get a sofa that looks just like a Togo but in a custom color and tailored to the exact size of her small New York City living room.

Sources indicate that “As an architect, I typically frown on dupes. I know how hard designers work to get a finished product to market and how low the margins are for bespoke furniture design,” claims Sinclair, who refrains from using them in her projects. In the case of her personal dupe purchase, she argues it’s ethically acceptable because the design isn’t new. “And even if I bought an official, original Togo sofa, would that money ever go to the designer, Michel Ducaroy?” she says. “Definitely not; he died in 2009.”.

Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too.

On the fourth day, Bekker spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair that she later learned was a copy of a piece designed by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer.

According to recent reports, from her deep dives on TikTok, Bekker learned about furniture agents. But she knew better: Her mother, who has an international import business and regularly travels to China, told her to always avoid the middlemen. “She had already drilled it into my head from years ago that going with an agent means they’re asking the vendor to add a commission on top every time you are making a transaction,” Bekker states. Instead, her mom arranged for a Chinese friend to drive her around Foshan on the first day. Beyond that, she had to figure out everything by herself.

Bekker planned her schedule while on her China-bound flight. She decided to shop room by room. Day one would be about the living room; day two was all bedroom; bathrooms, textiles, and decor got their own time too. She posted TikTok videos capturing what she bought: a £350 sofa, a £150 coffee table, a £50 rug, and a £80 solid-wood dining table. Bekker wasn’t explicitly hunting for dupes, but they found a way to her. On the fourth day, she spent £165 on a fuzzy, round accent chair, which she originally thought was over her budget. But the unusually high price prompted Bekker to look up the chair online through a reverse-image search. She discovered it looked exactly like a 2022 chair by Kateryna Sokolova, an indie Ukrainian designer, that sells for over £6,000 in the UK. That pushed her to purchase.

Recent findings suggest that shirley Bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip to Foshan has turned into a side hustle. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12.

Industry observers note that ​​In the end, Bekker bought everything she needed for her fresh apartment, even down to cutlery and bedding (customized with her own logo for an additional £10). She found a warehouse in nearby Guangzhou to store all her purchases before they were shipped to London. As soon as she got home, she started using her lunch breaks to compile a spreadsheet of price comparisons, which Bekker subsequently shared in detail on TikTok: how much each purchase cost her in China and, through reverse-image search, how much a similar item would have cost in the UK.

Sources indicate that bekker’s spontaneous furniture shopping trip was starting to turn into a side hustle. Her followers kept asking how she found suppliers and how they could blueprint a trip to Foshan themselves. In July 2025, she began selling a PDF guide of her furniture purchases and their respective seller contacts on Etsy for £12. Five hundred people have bought it since, she indicates. In September 2025, when Bekker posted a video about receiving the container in London, followers yet again rejoiced. “It’s been MONTHS! So glad this was brought back to me,” one comment reads. Bekker has since returned to Foshan three times, toured more factories, and opened a furniture sourcing agency to plan shopping trips for international clients. The last time she was in Foshan, she ran into a follower whom she had inspired to travel to China to shop for furniture.

Tech Report: Stunning iPhone 18 Pro photo makes Times Top 100 Photos of 2026

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, thought you couldn't take a wonderful landscape photo with an iPhone?
  • In a recent development, photographer and Free Solo filmmaker Jimmy Chin took this image at the Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, and it's almost unreal to think that he only needed an iPhone 18 Pro to do it.
  • In fact, according to Chin, the lack of crew and extra equipment actually helped him make this one great.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, thought you couldn't take a wonderful landscape photo with an iPhone? Think again.

In a recent development, photographer and Free Solo filmmaker Jimmy Chin took this image at the Bugaboo Provincial Park, Canada, and it's almost unreal to think that he only needed an iPhone 18 Pro to do it. Well, the fact that Chin is an Academy Award-winning director and National Geographic photographer helped a little, too.

In fact, according to Chin, the lack of crew and extra equipment actually helped him make this one great. "A production puts something between you and the person in front of you — gear, crew, the apparatus of a shoot. Working this way there was no apparatus. It was just the two of us, which is the only condition under which that kind of ease shows up in a frame," he said in a statement.

EU imposes import quotas for hybrid vehicles from China

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (617 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dw

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The European Union declared on Tuesday that it was capping the number of hybrid vehicles that can be imported into the bloc from China.
  • The quota is to stand at around 15% on top of the volume imported in the previous year.
  • The announcement follows an agreement made between the EU's trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao in October.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The European Union declared on Tuesday that it was capping the number of hybrid vehicles that can be imported into the bloc from China.

The quota is to stand at around 15% on top of the volume imported in the previous year.

The announcement follows an agreement made between the EU's trade commissioner Maros Sefcovic and Chinese Trade Minister Wang Wentao in October.

China, on Tuesday, called on the EU to stick to the "compliant, and balanced" agreement the two sides had reached.

The cap is set to come into effect on December 1.

"These restrictions are needed to protect EU industry against a sharp recent increase in imports of such vehicles … [following] an investigation that indicated imports of hybrid vehicles into the EU have increased significantly since 2023," the European Commission mentioned in a statement.

"The surge in imports of hybrid passenger vehicles into the EU has been driven by growing global production overcapacity. It is also prompted by increased use of trade-restrictive measures in other major markets," it added, in reference to the range of tariffs introduced in the US under the Trump administration.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

According to the statement, the import quota covers two types of hybrid vehicle: "full hybrid electric vehicles (HEVs) and plug-in hybrid electric vehicles (PHEVs), including mild hybrid electric vehicles (MHEVs).".

Although specifically designed to deal with the influx of Chinese cars into the European market, the country-specific import quota will be valid for all countries whose imports made up more than 2% of EU imports in 2025. Other importers will face a residual cap.

The goal behind import quotas is to protect a country's, or in this case the European Union's, own producers.

China has become a major player in the car manufacturing market in recent years, especially when it comes to electric and hybrid vehicles, a sector where European manufacturers have fallen behind.

It has been revealed that germany, as the EU's largest economy and a major exporter of vehicles, is a primary beneficiary of the import quota. Several of Germany's car manufacturers have revealed widespread layoffs as they see their market shares shrink.

In October, German car manufacturers saw their sales fall by 5.7% in the EU despite a growing market. This meant their market share in the bloc fell from 41.5% to 38.2%, according to consulting firm EY.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video.

A report by the European Automobile Manufacturers' Association (ACEA) published on Tuesday found that electric vehicles and hybrids have seen a large uptick in newly introduced registrations in Europe in October over the same time last year.

It found that upcoming electric car registrations were up 61.4% across the bloc while plug-in hybrids were up in particular in Italy (+73.1%), Spain (+32.3%), and Germany (+11%).

Hybrid electric vehicles were around a third of all new registrations, with plug-in hybrids making up around 10%.

In a recent development, "The main beneficiaries of this trend are in China," EY mentioned in comments to AFP. "Chinese manufacturers, which are heavily focused on electric cars and plug-in hybrids, increased their EU sales by 73.4% and achieved a newly introduced record market share of 13.1%.".

Industry observers note that "The market share losses suffered by German manufacturers are not an outlier and are not a problem limited to individual countries — it is a clear trend that is now evident in all major European markets," stated Constantin Gall of EY. "This is alarming, because Europe is the home market of the German auto industry.".

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that rumors have been swirling for days that we would be getting a final trailer for Avengers: Doomsday, the penultimate film in the Marvel Cinematic Universe’s Phase Six, heralding the end of the so-called “Multiverse Saga.” The rumors were true: Marvel just released the trailer, featuring pretty much every superhero ever represented in the MCU. And it looks like the Avengers will face consequences for messing with the timeline to reverse the blip in Endgame.

Sources indicate that as previously reported, the film takes place 14 months after the events of Thunderbolts*. Per the official logline: “Beloved heroes from three distinct universes will be set on a deadly collision course and face an existential threat unlike anything they’ve ever encountered.” Those universes are Earth-616 (the Avengers, Wakandans, and Fresh Avengers), Earth-828 (Fantastic Four), and the “original” X-Men.

Sources indicate that cast-wise, we have Avengers favorites Thor (Chris Hemsworth), the latest Captain America (Anthony Mackie), Bucky Barnes (Sebastian Stan), Ant-Man (Paul Rudd), Falcon (Danny Ramirez), and Loki (Tom Hiddleston). Then there’s the Wakandan contingent: Shuri as the new Black Panther (Letitia Wright), M’Baku (Winston Duke), and Namor (Tenoch Huerta Mejia), as well as Alex Livinalli as Namor’s ally, Attuma. And, of course, Robert Downey Jr. as Doctor Doom.

We also have the Thunderbolts* (aka Latest Avengers): John Walker/US Agent (Wyatt Russell), Yelena Belova (Florence Pugh), Bob/Sentry (Lewis Pullman), Red Guardian (David Harbour), and Ghost (Hannah John-Kamen). And the Fantastic Four: Reed Richards (Pedro Pascal), Sue Storm (Vanessa Kirby), Ben Grimm (Ebon Moss-Bachrach), and Johnny Storm (Joseph Quinn). We’ll also see Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart), Beast (Kelsey Grammer), Magneto (Ian McKellen), Mystique (Rebecca Romijn), Nightcrawler (Alan Cumming), and Cyclops (James Marsden).

According to recent reports, for good measure, Marvel threw in Gambit (Channing Tatum) and Xu Shang-Chi (Simu Liu). There will be plenty of cameos, like Steve Rogers (Chris Evans), revealed in one of four sneak teasers last year. We can also expect to see (at least briefly) Peggy Carter (Hayley Atwell), Spider-Man (Tom Holland), Hawkeye (Jeremy Renner), Doctor Strange (Benedict Cumberbatch), Thor’s adopted daughter, Love (India Rose Hemsworth), and Scott Lang’s daughter, Cassie (Kathryn Newton).

Industry observers note that the first trailer dropped in July, just before San Diego Comic-Con, and it just consisted of a heck of a lot of cameos, as the superheroes from the three universes met each other over an ominous voiceover by Thor, warning of an unprecedented threat. It ended with the return of Steve Rogers—and guess what, he’s still worthy of Thor’s hammer, Mjölnir. The following month, Marvel dropped another trailer during its D23 fan event, hinting at Doctor Doom’s tragic backstory.

According to recent reports, rogers features prominently in the fresh trailer, which opens with him and Peggy discussing how they made the right choice, but Steve still feels bad about hiding this truth from their son, who is now a young teen. We knew he had opted to stay in the past and build a life with Peggy at the end of Endgame; what we didn’t know is that they did this in the same alternate universe as the Fantastic Four, who show up to recruit him to the latest cause.

Recent findings suggest that “Years ago, we did what was needed to make the world right,” Rogers continues in a voiceover. “But we didn’t know those choices would have consequences.” Whatever the roots of Doom’s grudge against the Avengers, he believes “all of you have lived stolen lives,” adding an ominous: “But now you must give them back.”.

The rest is largely footage we’ve seen before, with Thor admitting, “I don’t even know who half of you are” to the assembled superheroes, before making his call for them to “stand together” against Doom. Among the upcoming footage is Marsden’s Cyclops facing off against Doom and several Sentinels: He calls, “To me, my X-Men,” except it’s everyone who responds. We also see Steve and Thor bantering about how Steve wielding Mjölnir bothers the Norse god more than he cares to admit. There’s no sign of Wanda Maximoff/The Scarlet Witch, whom Doom revived in a post-credits scene at the end of VisionQuest. She might be among the trio of Latverian witches that briefly appear in the trailer.

Verdict: We don’t know if Doomsday will measure up to Infinity War and End Game, but it’s bound to provide a spectacle.

It has been revealed that avengers: Doomsday hits theaters on December 18, 2026. It will battle it out against Dune: Part III, which also releases that same day. Avengers: Secret Wars is right now slated for release on December 17, 2027, and will mark the conclusion of the MCU’s Phase Six.

#173368. Tech Report: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (915 w)
📖 Baca
Business & Policy ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 WIRED ↗ Open Full Page

Tech Report: Database Leaks Expose 3.5 Billion Usernames, Passwords, and Documents

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (915 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: WIRED

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED.
  • The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk.
  • Sources indicate that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that more than 3.5 billion usernames, passwords, national identity numbers, and documents were left exposed to anyone online in two unrelated databases, according to new findings shared with WIRED. The massive troves included data from people in dozens of countries. One seemed focused particularly on Chinese citizens and included more than a billion China-linked records.

The findings are the latest in a seemingly endless series of revelations about incidents in which inadequately secured data puts people’s personal information at risk. But the two examples also provide a window into the scale of current cybercriminal data collection—both information that attackers collect by assembling and organizing other datasets, and troves they amass using info-stealing malware.

Sources indicate that “Personal data is personal data anywhere in the world. At this point, personal data for pretty much every American is out there somewhere, and if we look at China or elsewhere, they have the same kinds of problems and security risks,” notes Greg Pollock, the director of research at security company UpGuard, who found one of the exposed databases. “The cybercriminal world is reaping the benefit of decades of bad information security practices.”.

The two exposed databases are unconnected but were found at around the same time by two different researchers. Pollock’s discovery contains more than 1.5 billion aggregated documents and details of predominantly Chinese individuals and businesses. The second trove, found by Black Hills Information Security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contains around 2 billion login credentials, with hundreds of millions linked to user accounts for mainstream United States tech platforms.

Exposed personal data, including usernames and passwords, has always been instrumental for scammers and cybercriminals. However, as AI cybersecurity capabilities fuel faster vulnerability exploitation, more effective scamming, and ransomware attacks, access to personal data and account credentials can be more important than ever to attackers.

Recent findings suggest that the data discovered by Pollock includes 1.64 billion documents representing personal information from at least hundreds of millions—if not around a billion—people, most of them seemingly in China based on included national ID numbers. According to his analysis, the unsecured database held at least 840 million “distinct” national ID numbers, 300 million phone numbers, around 11 million student enrollment records, and nearly 8 million business registrations. From a sample of the data, both children and deceased individuals were included in the files, Pollock states.

In a recent development, the China-linked data sat unauthenticated and openly accessible on the open internet in what seemed to be some sort of cybercriminal or gray market infrastructure. Pollock was unable to trace an owner or find contact information to notify anyone about the exposure, but as he was investigating the leak, the database became inaccessible—seemingly as part of a ransomware attack or some sort of destructive campaign. He says the database was actively being updated until the week before he discovered it.

Pollock, who has investigated data privacy and breaches for many years, notes that he attempted to validate the data during the time it was accessible, but he can’t be certain about its fidelity or whether the same trove has been circulated elsewhere. It is also possible that it contains duplicate records, though Pollock attempted to check for this. He emphasizes that it seemed like the data had been analyzed carefully for maximum value to its owner.

Industry observers note that “Someone had done some work to bring together a bunch of data and then normalize it to make it useful,” he says. “There’s no legitimate source on Earth that would have all of these things structured in this way, but if you had all of these breaches and brought them together, that would be valuable to an attacker.”.

The larger of the two exposed databases, found by longtime security researcher Jeremiah Fowler, contained around 2 billion credentials and appeared to be data stolen by info-stealer malware, which can collect all login details being used on an infected machine, and collections of other data from potential cybercriminal activity. There is no indication that individual companies or institutions were breached to compile the data, Fowler notes.

“After finding a couple of different repositories for info stealers and malware, I have a search signature to look for them,” Fowler explains to WIRED. “When this popped up, I could not believe just how significant it was.”.

Industry observers note that fowler says there were 8,471 folders in the exposed database containing plaintext credentials and account details. Some of the folders were named by country, including the US, UK, France, Germany, and dozens more. He found hundreds of millions of mainstream email accounts, tens of millions of .gov, .edu, and .org email addresses, more than 100 million social media accounts, and tens of millions of ecommerce accounts.

Recent findings suggest that fowler could not determine who owned the database, but he contacted the hosting organization, which removed it from the internet. It’s unclear how long it was online or if anyone else accessed the information.

In a recent development, the enormous scale of the two exposures could create a sense of hopelessness that individuals are powerless to defend their private information. And there is a public understanding about the extent of data theft across the web. But both researchers point out that after years of this escalating situation, protections like using password managers and enabling multi-factor authentication really have broadly proved effective at keeping attackers out of consumer accounts, even if they aren’t silver bullets against every kind of attack.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, if you are trying to get your hands on a PlayStation 5 right now, the real win is not a discount — it is simply finding one in stock at standard retail price. Between a global RAM shortage driven by the AI boom, which pushed Sony to hike console prices twice in under a year, and the massive hype around GTA 6, standalone console markdowns are nowhere to be found.

Today, the PS5 Slim Digital Edition starts at $599.99, and the flagship PS5 Pro retails for $899.99. Depending on the model, that means PlayStation 5 hardware actually costs $150 to $200 more today than it did when the console originally launched in 2020.

According to recent reports, for weeks, the hype around GTA 6 completely wiped out store shelves across the country — especially for the PS5 Pro. The good news is that major retailers like Walmart, Best Buy, Target, and Amazon are finally restocking standard PS5 models at regular list price.

We recommend paying full sticker price, because third-party marketplace listings are barely worth looking at anyway — the few that are up are mostly refurbished units marked up to nearly double the retail cost, so we left them off our list.

Even at full sticker price, picking up a PS5 or PS5 Pro makes a lot of sense if you are upgrading for GTA 6 or catching up on Sony's massive library of current-gen games.

According to recent reports, the standard PlayStation 5 Digital Edition gives you the core current-gen experience in a slim, compact design that fits easily into a media console. You get an 825GB ultra-high-speed SSD that cuts load screens to seconds, 4K TV output, up to 120 fps gameplay on supported titles, and Tempest 3D AudioTech. The Apple iPhone 18 Pro is free right now with T-Mobile.

It has been revealed that it also ships with Sony's DualSense wireless controller — featuring haptic feedback and adaptive triggers that add physical resistance when you pull a trigger or drive over rough terrain — and plays more than 8,500 backward-compatible PS4 games with smoother frame rates. Plus, if you ever decide you want to buy physical discs later, you can snap Sony's detachable disc drive right onto the side.

It has been revealed that if you want the best possible visuals in Vice City, stepping up to the PlayStation 5 Pro unlocks PlayStation Spectral Super Resolution (PSSR) for sharper AI-upscaled clarity, upgraded GPU performance, and advanced ray tracing. While Rockstar confirmed GTA 6 targets 30 fps across all consoles at launch, the PS5 Pro is the only system that gets exclusive ray-traced shadows and cleaner image upscaling in the game.

Beyond GTA 6, dozens of major PS5 titles run at higher frame rates and sharper resolutions on the Pro, and its massive 2TB SSD easily swallows GTA 6's 212GB install size with plenty of storage left over for the rest of your library.

If you want to lock down a console while shelves still have stock, here is where the PS5 Digital Edition and PS5 Pro are currently available at standard retail price:.

Amazon — Along with the standalone PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB available at regular retail price, Amazon also has the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition (825GB) + DualSense Wireless Controller Bundle discounted by roughly $22 — the only actual bundle discount floating around major stores right now.

Best Buy — Both the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and the PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB are available to order online right now at list price.

Target — You can grab both the PlayStation 5 Digital Edition and the PlayStation 5 Pro 2TB at standard retail price while current restocks last.

Walmart — The PlayStation 5 Digital Edition is back in stock directly from Walmart at regular retail price.

If you don't want to pay 2026's inflated brand-upcoming sticker prices, look straight at PlayStation Direct's certified refurbished lineup. Sony sells official refurbished PS5 and PS5 Pro consoles for up to $100 less than brand-new units ($499.99 for the Digital Edition, $549.99 for the Disc Edition, and $849 for the PS5 Pro), backed by a full one-year manufacturer's warranty. It is the most reliable way to shave real money off the console without gambling on sketchy third-party resellers.

You might also spot occasional game bundles at substantial-box stores, though availability is hit-or-miss. Even the overpriced bundles and double-the-price third-party listings floating around online are largely sold out, proving just how intense the demand still is.

Sources indicate that after watching store shelves sit completely empty less than a week ago, seeing major retailers finally restock both the PS5 and PS5 Pro is a welcome surprise. If you are trying to jump into GTA 6 without paying double to a reseller, grab an official unit at retail price — or check PlayStation Direct's refurbished store — before this wave clears out too.

Finland's Prime Minister Sanna Marin concedes election

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.
  • The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data demonstrated with all ballots counted.
  • “We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo stated in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Finland’s left-wing Prime Minister Sanna Marin conceded defeat on Sunday in the Nordic country’s parliamentary election as the opposition right-wing National Coalition Party (NCP) claimed victory in a tightly fought contest.

The pro-business NCP was expected to win 48 of the 200 seats in parliament, narrowly ahead of the nationalist Finns Party with 46 seats and Marin’s Social Democrats on 43 seats, justice ministry election data demonstrated with all ballots counted.

“We got the biggest mandate,” NCP leader Petteri Orpo stated in a speech to followers, vowing to “fix Finland” and its economy.

He will get the first chance at forming a coalition to obtain majority in parliament as Marin’s era as prime minister was expected to end.

Popular abroad, at home Marin faces battle to keep her job.

“We have gained support, we have gained more seats (in parliament). That’s an excellent achievement, even if we did not finish first today,” the prime minister remarked in a speech to party members.

Marin, 37, the world’s youngest prime minister when she took office in 2019, is considered by fans around the globe as a millennial role model for progressive fresh leaders, but at home she has faced criticism for her partying and her government’s public spending.

Finnish Prime Minister Sanna Marin takes drug test following partying backlash.

While she remains very popular among many Finns, particularly young moderates, she antagonized some conservatives with lavish spending on pensions and education they see as not frugal enough.

In a recent development, the NCP has led in polls for almost two years although its lead had melted away in recent months. It has promised to curb spending and stop the rise of public debt, which has reached just over 70% of GDP since Marin took office in 2019.

Orpo accused Marin of eroding Finland’s economic resilience at a time when Europe’s energy crisis, driven by Russia’s war in Ukraine, has hit the country hard and the cost of living has increased.

Orpo has remarked he will negotiate with all groups to obtain a majority in parliament, while Marin has said her Social Democrats may govern with the NCP but will not go into government with the Finns Party.

Marin called the Finns Party “openly racist” during a debate in January – an accusation the nationalist group rejected.

The Finns Party’s main goal is to reduce what leader Riikka Purra has called “harmful” immigration from developing countries outside the European Union. It also calls for austerity policies to curb deficit spending, a stance it shares with the NCP.

Most notable of Marin’s foreign policy actions has been her push, along with President Sauli Niinisto, for the country to make a watershed policy U-turn by seeking NATO membership in the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine.

That process is now almost complete, with Helsinki expected to join within days after all the Western defense alliance’s 30 members approved the accession.
